evidence: Cic. Fin. 1.10: Latīnam linguam … locuplētiōrem etiam esse quam Graecam
terms.comment: Cicero holds it richer than Greek (Fin. 1.10). The neuter plural Latīna, things Latin, is Latin writing or study (Cic. Arch. 23; Quint. 1.1.14).

evidence: Liv. 25.39.12: ex Graecō in Latīnum sermōnem (Lewis & Short)

terms.comment: With verbs of knowing, speaking, writing and translating: Latīnē scīre, loquī, scrībere, reddere (see speak, a language). Latīnē loquī can also mean to speak correct Latin, or to speak plainly (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: correct Latin, Latinity; Latin as a subject
evidence: Cic. Att. 7.3.10: malus enim auctor Latīnitātis est
terms.comment: Classically pure, idiomatic Latin: Cicero follows Terence rather than Caecilius, ‘a bad authority for Latinity’ (Att. 7.3.10). Traupman’s Latin teacher is a Latīnitātis magister (p. 30).

phrases.latin: nam et Latīna aliquandō īnfāns utique nūlla nōveram, et tamen advertendō didicī sine ūllō metū atque cruciātū, inter etiam blandīmenta nūtrīcum et joca adrīdentium et laetitiās adlūdentium
phrases.english: for once, as a baby, I knew no Latin at all, and yet I learned it by listening, without any fear or pain, among the coaxing of nurses, the jokes of people smiling at me and the games of people playing with me

phrases.latin: nōn longē itaque Latīna subsequī dēbent et citō pariter īre
phrases.english: so Latin should follow not far behind, and soon the two should go side by side
